lesson.child_mission: Collecting and recording investigation data means measuring carefully, repeating when planned and writing results in a clear table as you go.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Why do two or three trials help more than one trial?

FEEDBACK
Repeats show whether a result was a fluke and give a fairer typical value.

WATCH FOR
Changing the measure mid-way (drops then “looks wet”) breaks the data set.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Run your planned fair test. Complete the results table with all trials. Note any odd result and whether you repeated it.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Collecting and recording investigation data means measuring carefully, repeating when planned and writing results in a clear table as you go.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Run your planned fair test. Complete the results table with all trials. Note any odd result and whether you repeated it. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: new object/context, two named observations, claim about data linked to that evidence.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample misconception: Changing the measure mid-way (drops then “looks wet”) breaks the data set.. Correction: Repeats show whether a result was a fluke and give a fairer typical value. with evidence.

Parent: Likely misconception: Changing the measure mid-way (drops then “looks wet”) breaks the data set. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses data. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about data, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept a new example with named observations and a claim–evidence link about data. Reject title-only labels with no observation. / Accept a misconception plus corrected claim and evidence reason for data. Reject wording changes that leave the same error..

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Absorbency test: Trial1 towelA 12 drops; Trial2 11 drops. Table columns: material | trial | drops | notes. Do not rely on memory later.

TRY FIRST
Why do two or three trials help more than one trial?

FEEDBACK
Repeats show whether a result was a fluke and give a fairer typical value.
teach_steps.explain:
Collecting and recording investigation data means measuring carefully, repeating when planned and writing results in a clear table as you go.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Changing the measure mid-way (drops then “looks wet”) breaks the data set. Correct the claim or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
